To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the antimalarial drug atovaquone is a high-affinity binder of human serum albumin, and that the high binding affinity of atovaquone to human serum albumin is driven by hydrophobic interactions.
the C3-substitution of the 1,4-napthoquinone core of atovaquone is essential for its high-affinity binding to human serum albumin.

the strong HSA complexation of ATOVAQUONE (ATQ) is hydrophobicity- and pH-dependent and that the binding of ATQ to the principal HSA drug binding sites is driven by hydrophobic interactions and electrostatic interactions.

the elucidation of the binding properties of the antimalarials ATQ, lapachol, lawsone and related hydroxy-1, 4-naphthquinones with human serum albumin.
the development of new methods for the investigation of drug-protein interactions, and also provides a new insight into the binding of antimalarials to HSA.
the development of new, complementary spectroscopic techniques to investigate the binding of small organic compounds to HSA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the binding of the antiparasitic ATQ to human plasma albumin is hydrophobic in nature, and that the hydrophobic interactions are primarily mediated through the C3-substitution.
HSA binding affinity and binding mode of 2-hydoxy-1, 4-naphthohydroquinone-type compounds are determined by the hydrophobic character of the C3 substituents.
ATQ and related 2-hydroxygenapthoquinones bind to both HSA drug binding sites with a high affinity, driven by hydrophobic interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the C3 substituent of ATQ is crucial in the strong binding of this drug to HSA and its subsequent transportation to the site of action, the mitochondria of Plasmodium parasites.
